name: model-view-controller
context: Web applications with server-side rendering requiring clear separation of UI, business logic, and data access layers
benefits: Clear separation of concerns between Model, View, and Controller
Parallel development acceleration: frontend and backend teams work simultaneously
High testability: Model and Controller can be tested in isolation without UI dependencies
Code reusability: Model and Controller usable with different Views
Modularity: components can be developed, tested, and maintained independently
Simplified debugging: architectural clarity points directly to bug source
Flexibility: easy to add new views or modify existing ones without touching business logic
tradeoffs: Controller complexity: can become bloated with too much business logic (Fat Controller)
View-Model coupling: views may become dependent on Model structure
Navigation logic burden: Controller must manage application flow
Classic MVC had tight View-Model coupling in early frameworks
Moderate scalability: monolithic deployment limits independent scaling of components
Potential over-complication for simple CRUD applications
Distributed complexity when scaling beyond single deployment
use_cases: Web applications with server-side rendering (Django, Rails, Laravel, Spring MVC)
Simple CRUD applications with straightforward data operations
Teams familiar with web frameworks needing rapid development
Applications requiring clear separation for maintainability
Projects where UI and backend teams work in parallel
RESTful API backends with traditional request-response pattern
avoid_when: Highly interactive UI with complex client-side state management
Real-time collaborative applications requiring WebSocket or bidirectional updates
Mobile or desktop applications (consider MVVM or MVP instead)
Applications requiring independent scaling of individual components
Systems with complex domain logic requiring layered architecture
High-throughput scenarios requiring event-driven or reactive patterns
component_types: Model: Data and business logic layer
View Template Engine: View rendering machinery
anti_patterns: Fat Controller: business logic accumulated in controller instead of Model
Brain Controller: controller contains excessive flow control logic
Promiscuous Controller: controller depends on too many services or handles too many routes
Brain Repository: repository contains excessive business logic beyond data access
Meddling Service: service layer improperly intercepts controller-model communication
Leaky Model: Model exposes internal data structures violating separation
Fat Repository: repository handles multiple entities losing cohesion
design_principles: Separation of Concerns: Model handles business logic, View handles presentation, Controller handles coordination
Single Responsibility: Each component has a distinct, focused purpose
Passive Model: Model should have no knowledge of View/Controller; Controller updates Model
One-Way Data Flow: User input flows through Controller to Model, then to View for rendering
View Independence: Multiple Views can display the same Model without mutual awareness
Controller Minimalism: Controllers should delegate business logic to Model or Services
Testability: Model and Controller testable in isolation without UI dependencies
best_practices: Keep Controllers Lean: Controller should handle request routing, not business logic
Single Entity Per Repository: Maintain cohesion by isolating data access per entity
Limit Controller Dependencies: Aim for ≤3 service dependencies per controller
Use Passive Model: Let Controller update Model rather than Model notifying View
Apply RESTful Routing: Map URLs cleanly to Controller actions
Validate Early: Implement server-side validation in Controller before Model updates
Test Model Independently: Write unit tests for business logic without UI dependencies
Use ViewModel Pattern: Create view-specific models to decouple business Model from View
Encapsulate Domain Logic: Keep business rules in Model, not scattered across Controller
Implement Proper Error Handling: Centralize error handling in Controller or middleware
